processing: A Sichuan jasmine tea. As with other jasmine greens, a green base is scented with fresh jasmine blossoms; exact methods vary by maker.
harvest_season: Not well recorded for this tea. As with other jasmine teas, the green base and the jasmine blossoms are gathered at different times.
appearance_dry: Green leaf mixed with pale dried jasmine flowers, as the name suggests.
appearance_liquor: Typically a clear pale yellow-green, as with other jasmine greens.
appearance_wet: Soft green leaf, with the flowers loose among it.
taste_profile: Jasmine leads, as in other jasmine greens, over a light, fresh green base.

brewing.notes: General advice for a jasmine green: a lidded gaiwan holds the scent, and water off the boil keeps the base from turning bitter.

vintage_note: As is usual for jasmine greens, it is sold as a recent-year tea, scented after the spring base is made, once the jasmine flowers, and is best drunk fresh. Xu Jinhua gave Sichuan Zhuyeqing exclusive authorisation for the name in 2008, so check who is selling a tea under it.
description:
Bi Tan Piao Xue, roughly snow drifting on a green pool, is a Sichuan jasmine tea named for what you see in the cup: white petals floating on clear green tea. Unlike most scented teas, it keeps its petals in on purpose.

The method is built around timing. Jasmine releases its scent at night, so buds are picked before they open and layered with fresh green tea, which soaks up the fragrance. The tea is fired the next day and then sealed for over a month. The base uses tender, pre-Qingming leaf.

Expect a clean jasmine note on a gentle green base, typical of good jasmine greens. Use water that is hot but not boiling, and short early steeps. Too hot or too long brings out bitterness and drowns the flower.

Buying is the tricky part, because the origin depends on the maker. Xu worked with local Xinjin jasmine in Chengdu, while Zhuyeqing uses pre-Qingming base tea from Emei and jasmine from Hengxian in Guangxi. A good petal scatter is pretty, but aroma from scenting matters more than decoration.
history:
Press accounts credit Xu Jinhua, known as Xu Gong, with the tea. He became head of the cultural centre in Xinjin county in 1971 and began making scented tea at home for friends and visitors. Friends, seeing white flowers float on the clear liquor like falling snow, urged him to name it.

In 2008, as demand outran his small output and counterfeits appeared, he gave Sichuan Zhuyeqing Tea exclusive authorisation for the name and passed on the method. In 2019 Xu took Qin Li and Xiao Ping as apprentices, as second-generation inheritors of the hand-scenting craft.
